Treasure in Heaven
TREZH-er in HEV-un
n. phrase (from Matthew 6:19–21; the eschatological wealth accumulated through single-hearted devotion to God rather than earthly accumulation)
Treasure from Old French tresor, Latin thesaurus, Greek thēsauros (storehouse, treasure). Heaven from Old English heofon (the sky, the dwelling of God). The phrase “treasure in heaven” appears in Matthew 6:20 and its parallel in Luke 12:33, and in the Rich Young Ruler pericope (Matthew 19:21; Mark 10:21; Luke 18:22). In each case Jesus identifies a form of eschatological wealth — permanent, imperishable, and located in God's domain — that stands in contrast to the perishable, stealable wealth accumulated on earth.

See also: Treasure in Heaven

Biblical Definition

The command to “lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven” (Matthew 6:20) is the positive counterpart to the prohibition against laying up earthly treasures — where moth, rust, and thieves reduce everything to nothing. Jesus identifies the heart as the index of where one's real treasure is: “where your treasure is, there will your heart be also” (6:21). The movement of desire reveals the movement of the soul; treasure-location diagnoses heart-location. The Rich Young Ruler passage (Matthew 19:21) makes the application concrete: “If you wish to be complete, go and sell your possessions and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven.” The exchange is not abolition of wealth-aspiration but relocation of it from the perishable to the permanent. The immediately following verse in the Sermon (6:22–24) develops the diagnosis: the eye that is “single” (or “clear”) toward God allows the whole body to be full of light; the divided eye, attempting to serve both God and mammon, produces inner darkness. Treasure-in-heaven theology is thus a doctrine of single-heartedness before God — the undivided devotion that Augustine called the ordering of loves (ordo amoris): God is the supreme good toward whom all other goods are rightly ordered. The Puritan tradition (particularly Richard Baxter's Saints' Everlasting Rest) developed this into a full program of heavenly-mindedness: the Christian invests mental and emotional energy in the contemplation of eternal goods, so that earthly goods are properly relativized rather than despised.

Webster 1828 Definition

Treasure in heaven (Matthew 6:20) names the eschatological wealth accumulated through single-hearted devotion to God — permanent, imperishable goods that thieves cannot steal and moth cannot consume — contrasted with earthly accumulation as the true object of Christian desire.

TREASURE IN HEAVEN, n. [Greek thēsauros en ouranō.] The eschatological wealth commanded by Christ in Matthew 6:20 as the object of Christian accumulation: imperishable goods located in God's domain, immune to moth, rust, and thieves, and permanently accessible. Contrasted with earthly treasures which are perishable, stealable, and corruptible.

Matthew 6:21 provides the heart-diagnostic: “where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.” The location of one's treasure reveals the location of one's heart. This makes treasure-in-heaven not merely a financial principle but a spiritual anthropology: the soul goes where it deposits its desires; heavenly treasure-deposit produces heavenly heart-orientation.

The “single eye” of Matthew 6:22–23 develops the same idea through the body's light-organ: an undivided eye directed toward God fills the whole body with light; a divided eye — trying to see both God and mammon simultaneously — produces inner darkness. Single-heartedness toward God is the condition of spiritual perception.

The Rich Young Ruler passage (Matthew 19:21) applies the principle pastorally: the ruler's treasure was his earthly wealth, and he could not relocate it to heaven at Christ's command. His departure “grieving” reveals that his heart had followed his treasure to earth; Jesus' command was not arbitrary poverty-advocacy but a diagnostic test of the heart's actual location.

Richard Baxter's The Saints' Everlasting Rest (1650) is the fullest Puritan development of the treasure-in-heaven doctrine: Baxter devotes the second half to “heavenly contemplation,” the practice of deliberately directing the mind toward eternal goods so that the affections are properly ordered. This is not world-denial but the reordering of loves: earthly goods are held lightly because better goods are held firmly.

Key Scripture

Matthew 6:19 — "Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal:"

Matthew 6:20 — "But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal:"

Matthew 6:21 — "For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also."

Matthew 6:24 — "No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon."

Modern Corruption

The prosperity gospel inverts the treasure-in-heaven command by promising earthly wealth as the evidence of heavenly favor; therapeutic evangelicalism reduces it to a life-balance principle; both suppress the radical single-heartedness and eschatological reorientation the command demands.

expand to see more

The prosperity-gospel tradition — Kenneth Hagin, Creflo Dollar, Joel Osteen — inverts the treasure-in-heaven command by reading it as a principle for earthly enrichment: give to God now and receive back multiplied earthly wealth as proof of divine favor. This turns the eschatological reorientation Jesus commands into a this-age investment strategy with divine returns. Jesus' prohibition on earthly treasure-accumulation becomes a financial vehicle for the very accumulation He prohibited. The gospel's “exceeding great and precious promises” (2 Peter 1:4) are eschatological promises, not stock-market guarantees; and the Rich Young Ruler demonstrates that Jesus does not promise earthly wealth to those who divest for Him but treasure in the age to come.

A subtler corruption in evangelical culture reduces treasure-in-heaven to a life-balance principle: don't make money your everything, hold it loosely, maintain perspective. This retains the surface counsel while defusing the radical command. Jesus does not say “hold earthly treasure lightly” as a balance correction; He says “do not lay it up” and commands its active relocation. The Puritan heavenly-mindedness tradition (Baxter, Sibbes) understood that treasure-in-heaven requires not merely loosened grip on earthly goods but active, deliberate investment of desire in eternal goods — a positive practice of contemplating and longing for heaven, not merely tolerating earth.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The treasure-in-heaven teaching flows from Old Testament Wisdom's deprecation of perishable wealth (Proverbs 11:28; 23:4–5), the Psalter's orientation toward the LORD as the soul's true portion (Psalm 73:25–26), and the eschatological inheritance promised to the new-covenant community.

expand to see more

Proverbs 11:28 and 23:4–5 — “He who trusts in his riches will fall”; “Do not weary yourself to gain wealth”; the Wisdom tradition's persistent deprecation of earthly wealth as a final good prepares the soil for Jesus' command to relocate treasure to an imperishable domain.

Psalm 73:25–26 (God as portion) — “Whom have I in heaven but You? And besides You, I desire nothing on earth.” Asaph's confession of God as the soul's all-sufficient portion is the experiential equivalent of treasure-in-heaven: the heart that has found its treasure in God has stopped competing with earthly treasures.

Matthew 13:44 (treasure hidden in a field) — the man who finds the kingdom of heaven sells everything he has to buy the field; the parable enacts what the command prescribes — total reorientation of treasure-desire toward the one thing of supreme value.

Luke 12:33–34 (parallel command) — “Sell your possessions and give to charity; make yourselves purses which do not wear out, an unfailing treasure in heaven”; Luke's version ties the positive command to concrete act of generous giving as the mechanism of heavenly treasure-accumulation.

Richard Baxter, The Saints' Everlasting Rest (1650) — the most sustained Puritan development of heavenly-mindedness: Baxter prescribes a daily practice of “heavenly contemplation” to keep eternal goods vivid and earthly goods in their proper subordinate place.

Usage

"The heart-diagnostic of Matthew 6:21 (“where your treasure is, there will your heart be also”) is the most searching test of true conversion: not what one professes but where one's desires go when unguarded reveals the heart's actual treasure-location."

"The Rich Young Ruler passage shows that the treasure-in-heaven command functions as a diagnostic test: Jesus did not give the same command to every petitioner (Zacchaeus was not told to sell everything), but He used it where the earthly treasure was the specific idol blocking the heart's access to the kingdom."

"Puritan heavenly-mindedness (Baxter, Sibbes) is the practical discipline Jesus' command generates: not passive detachment from earthly goods but active cultivation of desire for heavenly ones — the soul must be trained to find God more satisfying than what replaces Him."
